newsitem.title: PERU: Mothers and music mark 68th day of Peru crisis.
newsitem.headline: Mothers and music mark 68th day of Peru crisis.

text.p: An Argentine human rights group seeking to mediate in Peru's 68-day hostage crisis was rebuffed on Sunday when it tried to visit 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's home.

Police, meanwhile, added to their musical repertoire by blaring music from Beethoven to rock 'n' roll ahead of fresh talks on Monday to end the crisis. "It's like name that tune," said Reuters photographer Claudia Daut, keeping a vigil outside the besieged mansion in Lima's upscale San Isidro district.
Face-to-face talks between Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels and government negotiators are set to resume at 11 a.m. (1600 GMT) on Monday.
A delegation from the Buenos Aires-based Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo failed for a second day to breach police lines around the diplomatic compound.
Later they drove to a Lima women's prison to meet with rebel inmates but missed visiting hours. They were told to return on Monday, when they also plan to visit Lima's Castro Castro prison for men.

The group, famous for their struggle against Argentina's military rulers in the 1970s, does not plan to seek approval from uniformed authorities to visit either hostages or prisoners but wants to meet with President Alberto Fujimori.

"When there's a civilian government, you shouldn't have to ask permission of the military," Mothers leader Hebe de Bonafini told Reuters. Bonafini said the group will try to meet Fujimori again on Monday after failing to be received on Friday at Government Palace.

About 15 heavily armed MRTA rebels stormed the Japanese residence on Dec. 17, taking hundreds of VIPs hostage. They continue to hold 72, including Fujimori's brother Pedro and Peruvian and Japanese dignitaries and businessmen.

Sunday was another uneventful, albeit more melodic, day at the siege site. Police, using speakers placed outside the mansion, blared tunes ranging from opera and Mexican rancheras to easy listening and romantic rock ballads.
Since the start of the crisis, police have used music as a psychological weapon against the MRTA guerrillas as well as to alleviate boredom in the longest hostage crisis in Latin America's history.
Their tastes have evolved from military marches in the siege's early days to traditional guitar-based "criollo" waltzes and Sunday's rock and classical music.

Hostages, rebels, neighbours and the news media were treated Sunday to Beethoven and Vivaldi concertos, an opera sung by Placido Domingo, the "Theme from Love Story" and "Take My Breath Away" from the Hollywood movie Top Gun.
Later, one of three mediators in the crisis, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, held a mass for the hostages and a medical team visited the residence for more than three hours.
A Peruvian doctor said the hostages were mostly in good shape. "There is no one who is grave, who requires urgent attention outside the site," said Dr. Victor Lucero Rondon, himself a former hostage.

But the musical potpourri and the calm on Sunday masked the seriousness of the human drama as Peru's government and the MRTA readied for Monday's fifth round of preliminary talks in two weeks aimed at setting an agenda for formal negotiations to end the ordeal peacefully.
The rebels were demanding freedom for 400 jailed comrades. The government has rejected the demand but is willing to allow the hostage-takers to seek asylum abroad.
